chief_complaint: severe agonizing abdominal pain completely out of proportion to mild physical exam findings in cardiac patient
hpi_details: 74M with atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation presenting with sudden excruciating abdominal pain out of proportion to soft, non-tender abdominal exam, lactic acidosis, and bowel wall pneumatosis.
ideas: He thinks he came down with a violent bout of food poisoning from spoiled food he recently ate.
concerns: He is worried that an internal organ has ruptured and that he will not survive the day.
expectations: He hopes for immediate intravenous pain medicine to stop the unbearable agony and an emergency scan to see what went wrong.
pmh: Atrial fibrillation (off anticoagulation), hypertension, mild dyslipidemia

available_results.test: CT angiography of abdomen and pelvis
available_results.value: Embolic occlusion of the proximal superior mesenteric artery with pneumatosis of several small-bowel loops and reduced bowel-wall enhancement

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Mesenteric Ischemia (Arterial Thrombosis/Embolism) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Mesenteric Ischemia (Arterial Thrombosis/Embolism) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes immediate resuscitation with IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, urgent CT angiography for diagnosis, and emergent surgical or endovascular revascularization before irreversible bowel necrosis occurs, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe agonizing abdominal pain completely out of proportion to mild physical exam findings in cardiac patient

Key HPI features: 74M with atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation presenting with sudden excruciating abdominal pain out of proportion to soft, non-tender abdominal exam, lactic acidosis, and bowel wall pneumatosis.

Objective/Exam findings: Abdomen is soft and only mildly tender despite the patient's severe pain (pain out of proportion to exam) - a classic warning sign. Labs show elevated lactate (lactic acidosis) and leukocytosis. CT angiography demonstrates arterial occlusion and bowel wall pneumatosis suggesting early necrosis.
Relevant background/PMH: Atrial fibrillation (off anticoagulation), hypertension, mild dyslipidemia
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Mesenteric Ischemia (Arterial Thrombosis/Embolism).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Mesenteric venous thrombosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Pain out of proportion to exam findings — the classic warning sign.
management_principles: Initiate immediate IV fluid resuscitation and start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negatives and anaerobes
Obtain emergent CT angiography to confirm the diagnosis and localize the occlusion without delaying surgical consultation

Obtain emergent vascular/general surgery consultation for urgent revascularization (embolectomy, thrombectomy, or bypass) and resection of any non-viable bowel; initiate systemic anticoagulation once surgical bleeding risk has been addressed
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.assessment: Acute Mesenteric Ischemia (arterial thrombosis/embolism) with evidence of bowel wall pneumatosis - a time-critical surgical emergency.

learning_objectives: Recognize pain out of proportion to exam findings as the classic warning sign of mesenteric ischemia
Link atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation to embolic mesenteric ischemia risk
Prioritize emergent CT angiography and surgical consultation without delay given the time-critical nature of bowel viability
Outline revascularization and bowel resection strategies for acute mesenteric ischemia

teaching.one_liner: Sudden loss of blood flow to the bowel — often from an embolus in a patient with atrial fibrillation — causing pain dramatically out of proportion to a deceptively soft abdominal exam.
red_flags: Pain out of proportion to exam findings — the classic warning sign

must_ask.say: How severe is the pain, on a scale of one to ten?
Did the pain come on suddenly?
Do you have an irregular heartbeat, like atrial fibrillation?
Are you supposed to be taking a blood thinner, and have you been taking it?
Have you had vomiting, diarrhea, or blood in your stool?

history.answer: Doctor, my stomach started hurting out of nowhere, and the pain is absolutely unbearable. Please help me, I have never felt pain this terrible in my entire life.
It hit me all of a sudden about three hours ago while I was sitting at my desk. There was no warning at all; it just reached peak agony within minutes.
The pain is mostly around the middle of my belly, right around my belly button. It has stayed in the center and has not shifted anywhere else.
No, it does not shoot into my back, my shoulders, or down into my groin. It is locked right in the center of my stomach.
It is a constant, agonizing, gripping ache that feels like my insides are being crushed. It does not come and go in waves; it is relentlessly severe.
It is a ten out of ten, without question. It has stayed at that exact maximum level since it started.
Nothing I do makes it any better, whether I sit still, curl up, or walk around. I haven't tried eating, but just taking a sip of water made me feel sick.
I have had occasional mild indigestion after heavy dinners over the years, but I have never felt anything even remotely like this agony.
I felt terribly sick to my stomach as soon as the pain hit, and I threw up twice. It was just clear stomach juices, with no blood or dark coffee-ground material.
I had one loose bowel movement right after the severe pain started, but there was no visible red blood or black tarry stool. I have not passed any gas since then.
No, I haven't had any fever, sweats, or shivering chills. I just feel clammy from how bad the pain is.
No, my eyes and skin look their normal color, and my urine hasn't looked dark or tea-colored. My bowel movement was normal brown.
No burning when I pee, no need to run to the bathroom frequently, and no blood in my urine.
I felt lightheaded and weak when the pain first struck, but I did not pass out or lose consciousness.
No chest tightness, pressure, or palpitations, and no trouble taking a breath, except that breathing deeply hurts my stomach.
I just had plain oatmeal and black coffee for breakfast around four hours before this happened. I had one glass of wine two nights ago, but nothing today.
I took two extra-strength acetaminophen tablets when it began, but they did not touch the pain at all. I haven't taken any ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin.
I have an irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation that was diagnosed about two years ago, along with high blood pressure.
My cardiologist put me on a blood thinner called apixaban for my irregular rhythm, but I stopped taking it on my own about two months ago because I kept getting large bruises.
I thought I must have eaten some bad food that gave me a violent case of food poisoning.
The pain is so excruciating that I'm terrified something inside my stomach has ruptured and I'm not going to make it.
I just need something strong in an IV to take this agonizing pain away, and a scan to see what tore inside me.
Aside from atrial fibrillation, I have high blood pressure and mildly elevated cholesterol.
I have never had any surgeries, and I haven't been admitted to a hospital since I was a teenager.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure. I was supposed to be on apixaban 5 milligrams twice daily, but I stopped it two months ago.
I have no allergies to any medications, foods, or latex that I know of.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or nicotine products.
I only have an occasional glass of red wine with dinner once or twice a week, nothing heavy.
I work full-time as an accountant, and I live comfortably at home with my wife.
My father passed away from an ischemic stroke in his late seventies, and my mother had hypertension. No family history of bowel diseases or aneurysms.

exam.finding: The patient appears in severe distress, pale, diaphoretic, and visibly writhing in agonizing pain.
Blood pressure is 145/90 mmHg, pulse is 112 beats per minute and irregular, respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 97% on room air, and temperature is 37.1°C.
Irregularly irregular heart rhythm with normal S1 and S2 sounds, and no audible murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is flat and symmetric without surgical scars, distension, or visible peristaltic waves.
Bowel sounds are distinctly hypoactive in all four quadrants.
Abdomen is soft with only mild, vague periumbilical tenderness, and there is no involuntary guarding or rigidity.
No rebound tenderness or signs of generalized peritonitis.
Negative Murphy sign without localized right upper quadrant tenderness or cessation of inspiration.
McBurney point is non-tender; Rovsing, psoas, and obturator signs are all negative.
Normal anal sphincter tone with an empty rectal vault and no palpable masses, induration, or gross blood on the examining glove.
Radial and dorsalis pedis pulses are palpable bilaterally but irregularly irregular.
